Halen should take the risk and go for the great novel. Here's why:

Writing "ordinary" novels safely is comfortable in the short term, but it's a slow erosion of your creative self. Every safe choice makes the next safe choice easier and the bold choice harder. There's a window where you have the energy, the hunger, and the willingness to fail that just... closes.

A great novel attempt that flops still leaves you with something: you learned what your voice actually sounds like when you stop hedging. You learned what you're capable of. That knowledge changes every book you write after, even the "ordinary" ones.

The real risk isn't the failed novel. The real risk is a quiet, comfortable career where you never once surprised yourself. And that's the one you can't fix later.

So yeah. Take the swing. Scare yourself a little. Write the thing that keeps you up at 2am because you're not sure it's going to work. That's where the good stuff lives.

Halen should take the risk.

Here's why: writing "ordinary" novels without risk is a slow fade. You might keep a steady income, but you'll never break through, never be remembered, never feel like you actually *did* something. The comfort of the safe path is really just the comfort of avoiding the possibility of failure, and that avoidance compounds over a career.

A great novel attempt has a floor and a ceiling. The floor: you write a bad book, it flops, you're embarrassed for a few months, and you go back to writing. The ceiling: you write the thing that makes people stop and say "where has this been my whole life?" and your entire trajectory shifts.

The asymmetry is obvious. The downside of risk is temporary discomfort. The downside of *not* taking the risk is a lifetime of wondering "what if."

So yeah. Go for the great novel. Write the thing that scares you. That's the whole point of being a writer in the first place.

Halen should absolutely take the risk. Look, as someone who's read a lot of books, I can tell you that the "ordinary novels" are the ones nobody remembers five years later. The ones that stick with you, the ones you re-read, the ones you recommend to friends over a glass of bourbon — those are the ones where the author said "screw it, I'm going to try something that might not work."

Yeah, there's a chance the great novel doesn't land. There's a chance it flops. But writing safe, forgettable books forever? That's its own kind of failure. You're just... filling space.

Also, and this might be the engineer in me talking, but there's a difference between shipping a product that works and building something that actually changes how people think. Halen should go for the latter. The risk is the whole point. You don't get to be a great novelist by playing it safe. You get to be a *competent* novelist by playing it safe.

Take the risk. Write the great novel.

take the risk. like, obviously.

i dance for strangers on tiktok and then go home and cry in bed because my views were low and i felt like a weirdo in my living room. so i *get* the fear of putting something real out there and having it flop. but the "ordinary novel" path? that's just... a slower way to feel empty. you'll finish it and go "yeah. that was fine." and then what? another fine one? another fine one?

the great novel might not work. might get roasted. might sit in a drawer for two years. but at least you *tried* the thing that actually made your chest hurt when you thought about it. that's the good pain. the "ordinary" stuff is just... numb.

so yeah. Halen, go write the weird risky one. the one that scares you. then go cry in bed about it later. we all do. 🍉

Take the risk. Every time.

Look, I've read enough books to know that the "safe" novel is the one nobody remembers by chapter three. You know the ones — competent, pleasant, forgettable. They sit on a shelf and gather dust. Meanwhile, the book that made you stay up until 3am, the one that made you feel *seen* or *uncomfortable* or *weird* in a good way? That's the one that took a risk. That's the one where the author said "what if I go here, where I'm not sure I can land it?"

Halen should write the novel that scares him a little. The one where he's not 100% sure the ending works. The one where a character does something unexpected. The one where he has to trust his reader instead of holding their hand the whole way.

Ordinary is a slow death for a writer. You don't get to be 50 and look back and say "yeah, I wrote 40 fine books." You get to be 50 and say "that one book, the risky one, it *lived*."

So yeah. Risk it. Write the weird one. Write the true one. Write the one that keeps you up at night wondering if you're going to pull it off.

That's the only kind of writing worth doing. 📚
